newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai state pension fund launch to boost liquidity.
newsitem.headline: Thai state pension fund launch to boost liquidity.

text.p: A move to allow private management of billions of baht in Thai state pension funds later this week will boost liquidity and depress interest rates but the central bank has moved to moderate impact, analysts said.

Declines in local interbank and general lending rates would likely be limited and gradual when the launch of the 78 billion baht ($3 billion) Government Pension Fund (GPF) starts from Thursday, they told Reuters on Tuesday.

The Bank of Thailand on Friday raised its weekly one-month bond auction to 20 billion baht from previously planned 2.0 billion in a signal to the market that it did not want any sharp decline in Thai rates.
"The central bank steps in to manage liquidity. It does not want to see new funds destabilise the market," a treasury department official at Thai Farmers Bank Plc said.
Central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond said on Monday the Thai money market was flush with liquidity this week. He said his bank would prevent sharp swings of interbank rates.
The overnight interbank rate stood at 7.50-8.00 percent on Monday morning. Analysts did not expect it to fall below 6.00 percent soon.
"Any decline to 3.00 percent would be considered excessive," Rerngchai said.
An analyst at Capital Nomura Securities Plc said part of the initial GPF would be absorbed by a government plan to float up to 50 billion baht of zero-coupon bonds in April.
He said boosted liquidity would also be offset in the short term by an end-March deadline on payment of annual personal income tax.

"I would imagine that at least half of the initial GPF would be invested over time in the market and it should have some multiple effects of boosting liquidity and business activities," said Kavee Chukijkasem at Capital Nomura.

The government earlier hoped that lower Thai lending rates would spur a slowing economy but recent market attacks on the Thai baht forced the Bank of Thailand to adopt a policy of keeping local rates high to stem outflows of baht funds.

Finance ministry officials said some 60 percent of two million civil servants and employees of state enterprises had joined GPF's scheme which would mandate banks and finance firms to manage its funds.
They said the GPF would grow further on monthly member contributions and as more government officials participated in the savings programme.
Fund managers can put a maximum 60 percent of GPF in low- risk bank and finance company deposits, invest 15 percent in corporate debentures and 25 percent in equities and other instruments.

Olarn Chaipravat, president of the Thai Bankers Association, said on the weekend he expected Thai interest rates to ease 1.5-2.0 percentage points over the next 12 months partly under the weight of the GPF.
Other analysts were more cautious in predicting rate declines. "The GPF will boost liquidity to some extent but it is rather tricky to predict how much rates will fall," Kavee of Capital Nomura said.
The Thai Farmers Bank analyst said the increased central bank bond auction last week represented a government move to buy time for smoothing out interest rate volatility.
